name: Markifact
tagline: A hosted tool for turning markdown into clean, styled, shareable documents.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Markdown rendering is one of the most solved problems in software: the parsers, sanitizers, math renderers and diagram engines are all mature open source packages that an agent can wire together in an afternoon. The hard part of a product like this is not conversion, it is the typography, the theme set, and the hosted share links that make output feel finished. A personal build gets you 90 percent of the utility on day one: paste or drop markdown, pick a theme, export HTML or print to PDF. What it will not get you is a URL you can send someone without running your own server. If your use is private, local, and occasional, the paid tier is hard to justify; if you publish output to clients or teammates, hosting is the thing you are actually buying.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser app that renders markdown (including tables, code, math and diagrams) into a themed document you can export as HTML or PDF.
requirements: No accounts, no cloud services needed for the local build
A static host such as Netlify or a small VPS if you want public share links
whatYouLose: Hosted share links with stable URLs, so sending output to someone else means self-hosting
Professionally tuned themes and print typography, the thing that separates a document from a rendered README
Cross-device access and sync; your local build lives on one machine
Edge case handling in export pipelines: page breaks, footnotes, wide tables, font embedding
Someone else keeping up with markdown flavor quirks and dependency churn
moatNotes: The defensible part is taste in typography plus the boring plumbing of reliable PDF output. Neither is a network effect.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody wants to debug page breaks in a headless Chrome pipeline at 11pm before sending a document to a client. Paid markdown-to-document tools sell a short path from text to something that looks deliberate, plus a link you can hand to a person who does not have your toolchain. If you are producing documents for other people regularly, that is a real service. If you are producing them for yourself, a local renderer and your browser's print dialog cover it.
notes: Rendering markdown is free; making it look paid for is the product.
prompt:
Build a local-first markdown document studio as a single static web app. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS for app chrome only, document styles live in plain CSS files
- marked for markdown parsing, DOMPurify for sanitizing HTML output
- KaTeX for math, Mermaid for diagrams, highlight.js for code blocks
- Everything runs client side; persist state in localStorage

Features in scope:
- Split view: markdown editor on the left (plain textarea with monospace font and tab handling), live rendered preview on the right
- Drag and drop a .md or .markdown file to load it; also support paste
- GitHub flavored markdown: tables, task lists, strikethrough, footnotes, fenced code with language highlighting
- Support YAML front matter: parse title, author, date, theme and render them into a document header
- Three document themes as separate CSS files: "report" (serif, justified, numbered headings), "docs" (sans, generous line height), "paper" (academic two column abstract style, single column body). Theme switcher in the toolbar.
- Export buttons: download standalone .html with all CSS and fonts inlined, and "Print / PDF" that opens the browser print dialog against a print stylesheet with proper @page margins, page break avoidance inside code blocks and tables, and repeating table headers
- Table of contents generated from headings, toggleable, with anchor links
- Word count and estimated read time in a status bar

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, cloud sync, public share links, collaboration, mobile app, AI features.

Deliver: working npm scripts (dev, build, preview), a README explaining how to add a new theme CSS file, and three sample markdown documents in /samples that exercise math, diagrams, tables and code. No .env is needed since there are no secrets.
